Colorado GOP fields a historically disastrous slate for 2026, dominated by fringe figures and campaign scandals. 🌐
Evidence: Marx $57k fine, AI images, domestic violence disclosures
#Aletheia #USPol #Colorado

An opinion columnist argues that institutional campaign finance shifts and primary polarization hollowed out quality candidate vetting. 
Stated Judgement: (+0.5, 0.0) — Good Preference

The Republican primary base now rubber-stamps deeply flawed outsiders like Victor Marx, whose campaign is mired in fabricated credentials and abuse allegations. 
Resulting Judgement: (-0.85, -0.88) — Deception

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception. The Colorado GOP's collapse into fringe candidates and unvetted extremists reveals structural party decay behind nostalgic commentary.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 14.5, z: 2)

- Krista Kafer (Opinion): FAIL (0.50, 0.00) — Elegantly diagnoses decline while ignoring broader media complicity.
- Colorado GOP Nominees: FAIL (-0.95, -0.90) — Scandals, AI fakes, and domestic violence exposés.
Colorado Republicans face a devastating 2026 election cycle as fringe candidates like gubernatorial nominee Victor Marx implode under heavy scrutiny, ethics fines, and domestic violence revelations.

The Poison:
The nostalgia for old-guard party gatekeeping masks the uncomfortable reality that modern populist primary electorates actively reward sensationalism over competent governance.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing WHAT (the symptom of fringe nominees) with WHO (the radicalized primary voters and decentralized funding streams). The system rewards shock value over substantive qualification.

Social Physics Analysis:
Candidates like Victor Marx run Smart Selfish Maneuvers, using manufactured religious pretexts and AI-doctored images to project moral authority while concealing severe personal skeletons and campaign finance violations.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. Unchecked grievance politics hollows out institutional capacity until only fringe actors remain.

The Unavoidable Truth: Modern primary electorates increasingly reward sensationalism and fringe outsiders over seasoned public servants.

The Unavoidable Lie: Party leaders can easily restore top-down quality control without addressing deep-seated ideological polarization.

Alethekanon:
When party gatekeeping collapses under direct fundraising and ideological sorting, fringe extremism fills the vacuum. Nostalgia cannot resurrect a broken primary ecosystem.

Awwthekanon:
It is heartbreaking to watch the political process degrade into a spectacle of scandal and falsified images, leaving voters with painful choices and broken trust.

Brothekanon:
Imagine running for governor and getting busted for AI-generated rally crowds and old abuse stories. Colorado GOP's bench is practically nonexistent right now.

Spirithekanon:
"An evil man is snared by sinful speech, but a righteous man escapes from trouble." Proverbs 12:13 PASS 
When candidates build campaigns on falsehoods and fabricated images, truth eventually catches up and demolishes their pretensions.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
The Colorado GOP has fielded the saddest slate of candidates for statewide office in its history (Opinion)

It can’t get any worse for Colorado Republicans.

Actual Article Body:
Digital Replica Edition

Sign up for Newsletters and Alerts

Sign up for Newsletters and Alerts

Digital Replica Edition

Trending:

That which smells bad is rotten. Never again will I hold my nose to cast a vote. I once backed a contemptible candidate because we aligned on some issues. When he lost, he fomented violence to overturn the election, and his assault on the Constitution continues to this day.

As the Greek philosopher Heraclitus observed, character is destiny.

Unless yes is the answer to both of these questions, the oval beside the candidate’s name will remain unmarked: Do I largely agree with the nominee on public policy? Is the candidate of good character?

This November, there will be less ink on my ballot. For a variety of reasons that are easier to diagnose than to treat, the Colorado GOP has fielded the saddest slate of candidates for statewide office in its history — the high-quality contenders for state treasurer and attorney general notwithstanding.

In terms of campaign finance violations, wacked statements, resume fabrication, and uncloseted skeletons, Victor Marx officially outshines Dan Maes, the previous record holder for worst gubernatorial nominee, in every category.

Victor Marx, an unorthodox candidate, aims to harness AI and bring more accountability to the state as governor

Marx's recent $57,000 fine for receiving donations above the legal limit easily eclipses Maes' 2010 then-record fine of $17,500. Marx's tales of exorcism far surpass Maes' U.N. bicycle plot against America. Likewise, his claim of rescuing 45,000 women and children makes Maes' embellishments to his law enforcement resume seem unambitious.

The Marx campaign is better at manipulating images, as well. A press investigation revealed this week that video Marx plays when visiting churches contains footage pilfered from PBS of a human trafficking victim the candidate never met—fudging facts in church? Really? Another press investigation found the campaign posted an AI-doctored image of Marx at the Colorado State Fair Legislative BBQ. The AI provided the candidate what he lacked: a throng of enthusiastic supporters in the background.

Too bad for him, AI can't find and doctor old videos, not yet anyway. If party leaders blanched upon learning of Maes' past bankruptcy a month before the 2010 election, they must have turned a whiter shade of pale at this week's October surprise.

The Daily Beast released video of Marx lightheartedly recalling an incident where he slammed his wife into a door to teach her a lesson about the importance of martial arts training and another clip where he describes throwing his toddler son across the room.

Undecided voters can thank Marx for further unpacking his self-described "gift for violence," but these late disclosures only confirm what journalists at 9News and other outlets revealed before the primary.

Sadly, Marx is not the only 2026 candidate on the Colorado ballot who doesn't pass the sniff test. Election deniers Mark Baisley and James Wiley are running for U.S. Senate and Colorado secretary of state. Wealthy retiree Bob Chew figured he could skip lowly service in local and state elected offices, drop a few million on campy commercials, and win as a third-party Senate candidate. He should have bought a sailboat.

Try-try-again Greg Lopez is making a third attempt at the governorship this time as an independent. Both Lopez and Marx released video this week clarifying their roles in wife-shoving incidents. Alas, "If you're explaining, you're losing," to quote Reagan, particularly if the subject is domestic violence.

These deeply flawed candidates for governor, U.S. Senate, and secretary of state face Democrats with strong records of dedicated public service, and they will lose badly. The body may still be warm, but we can start the 2026 election autopsy now.

The Republican Party used to screen out candidates who lacked experience, told tall tales, embraced conspiracy theories, or had embarrassing skeletons in their closets. The once formidable state party that fielded successful candidates like Gov. Bill Owens and Sen. Hank Brown has become a rubber stamp for losers.

The Colorado GOP's death spiral wasn't caused by the petty party infighting of the past few years -- that clown show was but a symptom -- or by the strategic investments made by the "gang of four" beginning in 2003 to supercharge the Democrats' ascendancy, although that played a role, or by the Dan Maes debacle; that was but a sign of things to come.

The lethal infection can be traced to legal, technological, political, and demographic changes underway even when the party still appeared strong. Twenty-five years ago, party insiders could screen candidates for electability because candidates depended on political parties for funding, organization, communication, and media relations. Changes to campaign finance laws in the early 2000s made it easier for candidates to receive donations from PACs and advocacy organizations, while the internet enabled campaigns to connect directly to donors, supporters, and voters. The party as an institution that vetted candidates and forged consensus among coalitions became weaker as a result.

Meanwhile, both parties were becoming increasingly ideologically homogeneous. When I was a congressional staffer in the mid to late 1990s, there were liberal Republicans and conservative Democrats and a heterogeneity of policy preferences not seen today. As parties became more exclusively conservative or liberal, they strengthened their connections to groups according to ideology, interest, faith tradition, culture, sex and ethnicity. The party as an identity, or mega-identity, as Ezra Klein calls it in his insightful book Why We're Polarized, became stronger.

Blue states got bluer, red states redder as Americans began to seek like-minded communities. Once purple Colorado tipped blue, it got bluer as more Democrats migrated in and Republicans left. The state lost even more Republicans, as mainstream members, embarrassed by Trump's party takeover, became unaffiliated voters. While some continued to vote for right-leaning candidates in the general election, their involvement in the party ended. Now a narrow, ideologically driven base determines who wins the primary. More than 60% of GOP primary voters chose a fringe candidate (Marx or state Rep. Scott Bottoms) in June.

As the prospects for winning statewide declined, fewer quality candidates stepped up. Running for office takes an enormous amount of energy, money, and time away from family and work. Fewer people want to make that kind of life investment only to get sidelined in the primary by a nut candidate with a following or defeated by Democrats in the general. Likewise, donors, understandably wary of making risky investments, have decided to get more bang for their buck by donating to ballot initiatives.

So here we are. It can't get any worse for Colorado Republicans.

Why should Democrats care? Because the state is best run when there are competitive parties and the minority party can offer ideas, protect minority populations, and stop extreme legislation. No doubt Gov. Jared Polis had at times wished for a more balanced General Assembly during his tenure. Gov. Phil Weiser will, too.

Secondly, it is possible that Democrats are vulnerable to the same causes that slowly killed the state's GOP. The rise of candidates associated with the Democratic Socialists of America might be an early sign of trouble. Time will tell.

In the meantime, can anything be done to resurrect the Colorado Republican Party? That's a topic for another column, one I will likely not pen until Trump's toxic influence over the party is gone. As for this election, the best I can do is not participate in a tragedy that has become a farce.

63 years ago today, the second, and often considered best film starring James Bond, was released as From Russia With Love. In the film, Bond, played by Sean Connery, is sent to assist in the defection of Soviet consulate clerk Tatiana Romanova in Turkey, where SPECTRE plans to avenge Bond’s killing of Dr. No. by using […]
The post Good News in History, October 10 appeared first on Good News Network.

Actual Article Body:
63 years ago today, the second, and often considered best film starring James Bond, was released as From Russia With Love. In the film, Bond, played by Sean Connery, is sent to assist in the defection of Soviet consulate clerk Tatiana Romanova in Turkey, where SPECTRE plans to avenge Bond’s killing of Dr. No. by using Romanova as bait in a cleverly laid trap. The film was a critical and commercial success, grossing $78 million worldwide while critics found the film nonsensical, illogical, lurid, mad, and absolutely delightful because of it. READ more… (1963)

The British Film Institute’s screen-online guide called the film “one of the series’ high points” and said it “had advantages not enjoyed by many later Bond films, notably an intelligent script that retained the substance of Ian Fleming’s novel while toning down the overt Cold War politics (the Cuban Missile Crisis had only occurred the previous year).

The casting for the role of Tatiana included English, Italian, Swedish, Danish, and Polish actresses, but none who could actually speak Russian.

The score was written by John Barry traveled with the crew to Turkey at the request of the studio to try to get influences of the local music for the many scenes shot in Istanbul, but ended up using almost nothing apart from finger cymbals to give an exotic feeling, since he thought the Turkish music had a comedic tone that did not fit in the “dramatic feeling” of the James Bond movies.

Recalling his visit to Istanbul, John Barry once said, “It was like no place I’d ever been in my life. [The Trip] was supposedly to seep up the music, so Noel Rogers and I used to go ’round to these nightclubs and listen to all this stuff. We had the strangest week, and really came away with nothing, except a lot of ridiculous stories.”

More Good News on this Date:

19 years ago, Sheikh Muszaphar Shukor Al Masrie became the first-ever Malay to enter outer space when he rode up to the International Space Station aboard a Soyuz TMA-11 with the Expedition 16 crew. An astronaut and orthopedic surgeon, Alma Matter of Manipal University, Shukor Al Masrie performed experiments on live cancer cells to catalogue the effects of things like leukemia in space. He is the only Malaysian, representing the 20th nation, to visit the space station.

Since Sheikh Muszaphar is a Muslim, and as his time in space coincided with the last part of Ramadan, the Islamic National Fatwa Council drew up the first comprehensive guidebook for Muslims in space.

The 18-page guidebook is titled “Guidelines for Performing Islamic Rites (Ibadah) at the International Space Station”, and details issues such as how to pray in a low-gravity environment, how to locate Mecca from the ISS, how to determine prayer times, and issues surrounding fasting. The orbit of the ISS results in one day/night cycle every 90 minutes, so the issues of fasting during Ramadan are also addressed. (2007)

70 years ago today, the epic Western drama film Giant was released. Focusing on the struggle between wealthy oilmen and cattlemen in Texas in the mid-20th century, the film starred Elizabeth Taylor, James Dean, and Rock Hudson.

Giant was the final of Dean’s three films as a leading actor—and earned him his second Academy Award nomination, before he was killed in a car crash prior to the film’s debut. George Stevens won the Oscar for Best Director.

Martin Scorsese said in the 70s, “I’ve seen this film over forty times. There’s more here than people have seen. It has to do with the depiction of a lifestyle through the passage of so many years. You see people grow.”

A huge box-office success, the film’s earnings of $35 million for Warner Brothers were not surpassed until the 1970s with their release of Superman.

In the story, Dean is given a small plot of land, bequeathed by the rancher’s sister after her death. He toils until one day he strikes oil. He becomes wealthy, but rots inside from the unrequited love he maintains for the rancher’s wife through the decades, even after taking her daughter as a lover. The film also explores racism in the South, with Rock Hudson defending Blacks and Hispanics at the local cafe when they are unwelcome and thrown out. Another subplot centered around Taylor, who was raised on the East Coast, refusing to be deferential to men, as was customary in Texas, just because she was a woman. WATCH the scene where ranch hand James Dean strikes oil and express, in vain, his love for the rancher’s wife, Elizabeth Taylor… (1956)

And, on this day in 1902, the Gibson Guitar Company was formed in Kalamazoo, Michigan. It was founded with the intention to make mandolins, by Orville Gibson, a luthier with no formal training. The company ended up building one of the world’s most iconic guitars, the Gibson Les Paul in 1952—a solid-body electric instrument designed by their V.P. Ted McCarty and famed guitarist Les Paul.

Mr. Gibson invented the archtop design for his instruments, which made them louder and more durable, by constructing the same type of carved tops used on violins. The musical innovator never saw the riches that were distributed to the businessmen who took over the company, but only was paid for his hourly labor. By the 1930s, after Orville’s death, the company made one of the first commercially available hollow-body electric guitars, like the ES-150 popularized by Charlie Christian.

46 years ago today, Pac-Man first debuted—and it went on to become the highest-grossing video game of all time. The arcade game was deliberately designed to appeal to women as well as men, eschewing the popular war themes of the day, and instead using characters that were cute and colorful.

Its designer, Toru Iwatani, was 24 at the time and for a year led a small team of nine at his company (Namco, of Japan). With so many instant fans eager to gobble up all the dots in its maze, while avoiding the 4 ghosts, Pac-Man within a year had grossed over $1 billion in quarters.

The character named in Japanese after its shape—a hockey puck—generated more than $14 billion for Namco and is indeed the highest-grossing video game of all time. (1980)

And, on this day in 1868, Carlos Manuel de Céspedes issued the Grito de Yara in Cuba (the Cry of Yara), proclaiming Cuban independence, which began the “War of 10 Years”.

That morning, after sounding the slave bell (indicating it was time for his plantation slaves to work), they stood before him waiting for orders and Sr. Cespedes announced they were all free men—and invited to join him and his fellow conspirators in battle against colonial Spain. For this, he is called Padre de la Patria, Father of the Homeland.

Happy 57th Birthday to Brett Favre, the NFL football legend who became the first quarterback to throw for over 70,000 yards, complete over 6,000 passes, and tally over 500 touchdowns in his career.

At the helm of the Green Bay Packers for 16 years, he became the first player to win the league’s MVP Award three years in a row. A graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, where he grew up, Favre led the Packers to victory in Super Bowl XXXI and he also was the starting quarterback in an astonishing 297 consecutive games—321, including the playoffs, through 18​1⁄2 seasons—an all-time record, and the one for which he says he is most proud.

He joked around constantly and played the game like a kid, but Brett was the only athlete to become a grandfather while an active NFL player. After retirement, he became the offensive coach for a Mississippi high school that soon after won a state championship. (1969)

Twenty-five years ago, party insiders could screen candidates for electability because candidates depended on political parties for funding, organization, communication, and media relations. Changes to campaign finance laws in the early 2000s made it easier for candidates to receive donations from PACs and advocacy organizations, while the internet enabled campaigns to connect directly to donors, supporters, and voters. The party as an institution that vetted candidates and forged consensus among coalitions became weaker as a result.

Meanwhile, both parties were becoming increasingly ideologically homogeneous. When I was a congressional staffer in the mid to late 1990s, there were liberal Republicans and conservative Democrats and a heterogeneity of policy preferences not seen today. As parties became more exclusively conservative or liberal, they strengthened their connections to groups according to ideology, interest, faith tradition, culture, sex and ethnicity. The party as an identity, or mega-identity, as Ezra Klein calls it in his insightful book Why We're Polarized, became stronger.

Blue states got bluer, red states redder as Americans began to seek like-minded communities. Once purple Colorado tipped blue, it got bluer as more Democrats migrated in and Republicans left. The state lost even more Republicans, as mainstream members, embarrassed by Trump's party takeover, became unaffiliated voters. While some continued to vote for right-leaning candidates in the general election, their involvement in the party ended. Now a narrow, ideologically driven base determines who wins the primary. More than 60% of GOP primary voters chose a fringe candidate (Marx or state Rep. Scott Bottoms) in June.

As the prospects for winning statewide declined, fewer quality candidates stepped up. Running for office takes an enormous amount of energy, money, and time away from family and work. Fewer people want to make that kind of life investment only to get sidelined in the primary by a nut candidate with a following or defeated by Democrats in the general. Likewise, donors, understandably wary of making risky investments, have decided to get more bang for their buck by donating to ballot initiatives.

So here we are. It can't get any worse for Colorado Republicans.

Why should Democrats care? Because the state is best run when there are competitive parties and the minority party can offer ideas, protect minority populations, and stop extreme legislation. No doubt Gov. Jared Polis had at times wished for a more balanced General Assembly during his tenure. Gov. Phil Weiser will, too.

Secondly, it is possible that Democrats are vulnerable to the same causes that slowly killed the state's GOP. The rise of candidates associated with the Democratic Socialists of America might be an early sign of trouble. Time will tell.

In the meantime, can anything be done to resurrect the Colorado Republican Party? That's a topic for another column, one I will likely not pen until Trump's toxic influence over the party is gone. As for this election, the best I can do is not participate in a tragedy that has become a farce.

Krista Kafer is a Sunday Denver Post columnist.

63 years ago today, the second, and often considered best film starring James Bond, was released as From Russia With Love. In the film, Bond, played by Sean Connery, is sent to assist in the defection of Soviet consulate clerk Tatiana Romanova in Turkey, where SPECTRE plans to avenge Bond’s killing of Dr. No. by using Romanova as bait in a cleverly laid trap. The film was a critical and commercial success, grossing $78 million worldwide while critics found the film nonsensical, illogical, lurid, mad, and absolutely delightful because of it. READ more… (1963)

The British Film Institute’s screen-online guide called the film “one of the series’ high points” and said it “had advantages not enjoyed by many later Bond films, notably an intelligent script that retained the substance of Ian Fleming’s novel while toning down the overt Cold War politics (the Cuban Missile Crisis had only occurred the previous year).

The casting for the role of Tatiana included English, Italian, Swedish, Danish, and Polish actresses, but none who could actually speak Russian.

The score was written by John Barry traveled with the crew to Turkey at the request of the studio to try to get influences of the local music for the many scenes shot in Istanbul, but ended up using almost nothing apart from finger cymbals to give an exotic feeling, since he thought the Turkish music had a comedic tone that did not fit in the “dramatic feeling” of the James Bond movies.

Recalling his visit to Istanbul, John Barry once said, “It was like no place I’d ever been in my life. [The Trip] was supposedly to seep up the music, so Noel Rogers and I used to go ’round to these nightclubs and listen to all this stuff. We had the strangest week, and really came away with nothing, except a lot of ridiculous stories.”

19 years ago, Sheikh Muszaphar Shukor Al Masrie became the first-ever Malay to enter outer space when he rode up to the International Space Station aboard a Soyuz TMA-11 with the Expedition 16 crew. An astronaut and orthopedic surgeon, Alma Matter of Manipal University, Shukor Al Masrie performed experiments on live cancer cells to catalogue the effects of things like leukemia in space. He is the only Malaysian, representing the 20th nation, to visit the space station.

Since Sheikh Muszaphar is a Muslim, and as his time in space coincided with the last part of Ramadan, the Islamic National Fatwa Council drew up the first comprehensive guidebook for Muslims in space.

The 18-page guidebook is titled “Guidelines for Performing Islamic Rites (Ibadah) at the International Space Station”, and details issues such as how to pray in a low-gravity environment, how to locate Mecca from the ISS, how to determine prayer times, and issues surrounding fasting. The orbit of the ISS results in one day/night cycle every 90 minutes, so the issues of fasting during Ramadan are also addressed. (2007)

70 years ago today, the epic Western drama film Giant was released. Focusing on the struggle between wealthy oilmen and cattlemen in Texas in the mid-20th century, the film starred Elizabeth Taylor, James Dean, and Rock Hudson.

Giant was the final of Dean’s three films as a leading actor—and earned him his second Academy Award nomination, before he was killed in a car crash prior to the film’s debut. George Stevens won the Oscar for Best Director.

Martin Scorsese said in the 70s, “I’ve seen this film over forty times. There’s more here than people have seen. It has to do with the depiction of a lifestyle through the passage of so many years. You see people grow.”

A huge box-office success, the film’s earnings of $35 million for Warner Brothers were not surpassed until the 1970s with their release of Superman.

In the story, Dean is given a small plot of land, bequeathed by the rancher’s sister after her death. He toils until one day he strikes oil. He becomes wealthy, but rots inside from the unrequited love he maintains for the rancher’s wife through the decades, even after taking her daughter as a lover. The film also explores racism in the South, with Rock Hudson defending Blacks and Hispanics at the local cafe when they are unwelcome and thrown out. Another subplot centered around Taylor, who was raised on the East Coast, refusing to be deferential to men, as was customary in Texas, just because she was a woman. WATCH the scene where ranch hand James Dean strikes oil and express, in vain, his love for the rancher’s wife, Elizabeth Taylor… (1956)

And, on this day in 1902, the Gibson Guitar Company was formed in Kalamazoo, Michigan. It was founded with the intention to make mandolins, by Orville Gibson, a luthier with no formal training. The company ended up building one of the world’s most iconic guitars, the Gibson Les Paul in 1952—a solid-body electric instrument designed by their V.P. Ted McCarty and famed guitarist Les Paul.

Mr. Gibson invented the archtop design for his instruments, which made them louder and more durable, by constructing the same type of carved tops used on violins. The musical innovator never saw the riches that were distributed to the businessmen who took over the company, but only was paid for his hourly labor. By the 1930s, after Orville’s death, the company made one of the first commercially available hollow-body electric guitars, like the ES-150 popularized by Charlie Christian.

46 years ago today, Pac-Man first debuted—and it went on to become the highest-grossing video game of all time. The arcade game was deliberately designed to appeal to women as well as men, eschewing the popular war themes of the day, and instead using characters that were cute and colorful.

Its designer, Toru Iwatani, was 24 at the time and for a year led a small team of nine at his company (Namco, of Japan). With so many instant fans eager to gobble up all the dots in its maze, while avoiding the 4 ghosts, Pac-Man within a year had grossed over $1 billion in quarters.

The character named in Japanese after its shape—a hockey puck—generated more than $14 billion for Namco and is indeed the highest-grossing video game of all time. (1980)

And, on this day in 1868, Carlos Manuel de Céspedes issued the Grito de Yara in Cuba (the Cry of Yara), proclaiming Cuban independence, which began the “War of 10 Years”.

That morning, after sounding the slave bell (indicating it was time for his plantation slaves to work), they stood before him waiting for orders and Sr. Cespedes announced they were all free men—and invited to join him and his fellow conspirators in battle against colonial Spain. For this, he is called Padre de la Patria, Father of the Homeland.

Happy 57th Birthday to Brett Favre, the NFL football legend who became the first quarterback to throw for over 70,000 yards, complete over 6,000 passes, and tally over 500 touchdowns in his career.

At the helm of the Green Bay Packers for 16 years, he became the first player to win the league’s MVP Award three years in a row. A graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, where he grew up, Favre led the Packers to victory in Super Bowl XXXI and he also was the starting quarterback in an astonishing 297 consecutive games—321, including the playoffs, through 18​1⁄2 seasons—an all-time record, and the one for which he says he is most proud.

He joked around constantly and played the game like a kid, but Brett was the only athlete to become a grandfather while an active NFL player. After retirement, he became the offensive coach for a Mississippi high school that soon after won a state championship. (1969)
